articles.title: Newsom typically relishes battling Trump. On letting undocumented college students work, not so much.
articles.summary: In vetoing a bill that would have made immigrant students eligible to work, Newsom cited worries about retaliation from Trump.
articles.body:
Gavin Newsom has rarely shied away from a fight with Donald Trump, especially over immigration.

He didn't hesitate last year to sign into law a ban on federal immigration agents wearing masks in the state. And when he put his name on a package of legislation this year further clamping down on immigration enforcement, he said he was doing so to "push back on Trump's Orwellian immigrant tactics."

But when it came to a bill that would have required the state's public universities and community colleges to make undocumented immigrant students eligible for campus employment, Newsom balked.

Trump officials, he wrote in a message explaining his veto last month, are "quick to wreak destruction for political spectacle." The risk of them seeking retribution against the schools was too great.

Newsom's decision to avoid confrontation prolongs a yearslong student-led push to persuade skeptical university officials to enact a first-in-the-nation policy that would benefit the roughly 60,000 undocumented students enrolled in the three school systems. And it has deflated immigrant rights activists in his home state ahead of Newsom's likely presidential run.

"There's disappointment that on this issue, the governor hasn't been willing to take a risk for a very important part of the California population," said Maria Blanco, the former executive director of the UC Immigrant Legal Services Center. "Even in a progressive state like California, immigration sometimes still continues to be this third rail, especially if you're running for president."

The governor's unwillingness to force the issue with Trump stemmed, at least in part, from what he said in his veto message was a concern that the hiring requirement wouldn't hold up under legal scrutiny since federal law prohibits employers from hiring undocumented workers.

Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Newsom referred to the governor's veto message.

Advocates for the idea that students living in the country illegally should be permitted to work campus jobs have relied heavily on a legal theory a group of UCLA law professors published in 2022 that argued the federal ban doesn't apply to state agencies.

The theory was enough to spur discussion among the UC Board of Regents, which considered implementing a policy allowing the hires, but ultimately punted on the idea in 2024.

Rich Leib, the chair of the regents at the time who had signaled support for hiring undocumented students, said that enthusiasm on the board waned after three "established" law firms said they would not defend the university if its policy was challenged in court. With a second Trump term looming, Leib said a majority of the regents, including him, decided the timing was not right to challenge an administration that could be hostile to immigrants and voted to table the issue. They were particularly concerned, he said, about the possibility that immigration officials might be able to gain access to personal data about undocumented students on the university payroll.

"It was the most emotional experience I had as a regent because it brought you to people who were directly negatively affected by it," Leib said, referring to students who protested at the board meeting following the vote to shelve the plan. "These are people who have done really well their whole lives. They worked really hard to get where they did, and now you're telling them they can't get a job."

Joel Raznick, a regent emeritus who also voted for the delay, said that the possibility of Trump returning to the White House was "certainly on my mind." Raznick, who emphasized he was not speaking on behalf of the UC, said he had been concerned about the possibility the Trump administration would respond to the hiring policy by cutting federal funding to the university – a tactic it has used in other fights with the UC – and that undocumented students could be "readily identified and deported."

"I thought that we were doing a better service for undocumented students at that moment by preserving the university's ability to operate," Raznick said. "Because those risks are real, as we now know."

Anna Markowitz, president of the UCLA Faculty Association, which advocated for the hiring policy, pushed back on that rationale.

"Who are we allowing to suffer by claiming that we're saving the institution?" she asked.

Omar Rodriguez, a spokesperson for the UC, said that the university's "evaluation of this important issue is ongoing." He pointed out that the UC remained neutral on the bill Newsom vetoed.

"UC has been a leader in supporting undocumented students, who are vital members of the UC community and make significant contributions to our economy and society as scholars, researchers, and future leaders," Rodriguez said.

Along with the UC, the legislation would have applied to the California State University and community college systems. In statements, spokespeople for both systems said they also did not come out for or against the bill and support undocumented students while complying with state and federal laws.

Immigration advocates criticize Newsom and the regents for what they see as their overly cautious approach. Having a law on the books, they argue, would provide a layer of protection for the school systems if they were to have a policy allowing undocumented students to work on campus. They also point to a ruling in a state appeals court last year that found the UC's adherence to federal law forbidding employment was discriminatory. The ruling stated that the university could not rely on fear of federal retaliation as a reason for not adopting a more permissive stance, and ordered it to "reconsider its policy based on proper criteria."

"They're really caught in between a rock and a hard place," said Ahilan Arulanantham, a UCLA law professor who helped write the 2022 legal theory. "They have to comply with the state court decision, and they're not going to get the benefit of any California legislation protecting them from above."

The ruling, though, did not require the university to change its policy and did not include a deadline for the UC to comply.

"Large institutions tend to be risk adverse," Blanco said. "And I don't think this is a climate where the UC would affirmatively go do this and then wait to be sued."

articles.title: Nem todo eleitor que deixa de votar é desinteressado pela política | G1
articles.standfirst: Abstenção de 21% no primeiro turno bateu recorde, com 33 milhões de eleitores ausentes. Cientista político Jairo Nicolau explica por que o número não deve ser tratado como um grupo homogêneo.
articles.summary: Abstenção bateu recorde e chegou a 33 milhões de eleitores no primeiro turno. Cientista político Jairo Nicolau explica por que o número não deve ser tratado como um grupo homogêneo
articles.body:
Mais de 33 milhões de brasileiros deixaram de ir às urnas no primeiro turno das eleições de 2026. No entanto, esse número não pode ser interpretado como uma grande massa de pessoas desinteressadas pela política, afirma o cientista político e pesquisador da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV) Jairo Nicolau.

Autor do livro "O País Dividido", que analisa as últimas duas décadas de eleições no Brasil, Nicolau explica que o total de ausentes reúne pessoas com perfis e motivos diferentes para não votar. Isso inclui desde eleitores que não são obrigados a votar até aqueles que moram longe de seu domicílio eleitoral. Há também problemas de cadastro , como municípios com mais eleitores registrados do que habitantes.

Em entrevista ao g1 , o pesquisador afirmou que não é possível determinar quantos brasileiros deixaram de votar simplesmente por falta de interesse na eleição.

“A gente não sabe porque não há pesquisa”, disse. Segundo ele, os institutos costumam concentrar seus levantamentos nas intenções de voto, e não nas razões que levam parte do eleitorado a não comparecer às urnas.

Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada na sexta-feira (9) mostrou que viagem (19%), problemas de saúde (18%), desinteresse (13%) e trabalho (9%) foram os principais motivos do eleitor para não votar no primeiro turno.

Eleitores ouvidos pelo g1 em outra reportagem citam também a burocracia para transferir o título e questões de acessibilidade aos locais de votação como motivos para o não comparecimento.

A eleitora Bianca Dantas contou que, após passar por uma cirurgia no joelho duas semanas antes do primeiro turno, não conseguiu chegar à seção eleitoral porque não conseguia subir escadas. “Quantas pessoas deixaram de votar por essa mesma razão, né? Pessoas que sofreram acidentes, enfim, e isso foi muito frustrante para mim. Estar ali na porta e ter que virar as costas e ir embora sem poder votar”, disse. Leia a reportagem completa .

➡️No primeiro turno, em 4 de outubro, a abstenção ultrapassou 33,4 milhões de eleitores — 21,08% do eleitorado apto a votar — e atingiu o maior patamar desde 1998. O percentual teve uma ligeira alta em relação a 2022, quando 20,9% dos eleitores não votaram.

👉🏻 Abstenção é quando, mesmo tendo direito ao voto, o eleitor não comparece às urnas.

Nicolau esperava um pequeno aumento da abstenção neste ano, diante do que identificava como menor engajamento dos eleitores durante a campanha, a "campanha silenciosa". O percentual, porém, ficou praticamente no mesmo patamar de 2022.

“A gente está nesse patamar, mais ou menos 20 pontos, porque eu acho que tudo indica que é o padrão brasileiro de ausência das urnas”, afirmou.

No domingo (11), tanto Lula (PT) quanto Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) pediram a seus apoiadores que mantenham a mobilização no segundo turno. Em discurso na Paulista, Lula incentivou eleitores a tentar convencer quem não compareceu no primeiro turno a votar no dia 25. Flávio Bolsonaro se reuniu com prefeitos de cidades paulistas e alertou que sua campanha não pode "baixar a guarda" .

Nordeste e Norte tiveram menor abstenção

Nicolau analisou como a abstenção se distribuiu entre as regiões e os municípios brasileiros.

Para isso, dividiu os municípios em cinco grupos, de acordo com o tamanho do eleitorado. Cada grupo reúne aproximadamente 20% dos eleitores do país, ou cerca de 31 milhões de pessoas. Depois, separou as cidades de cada grupo pelas cinco regiões brasileiras.

A análise do pesquisador mostrou que o Nordeste registrou a menor taxa de abstenção neste ano, de 18,4%, seguido pelo Norte, com 19,4%. Os maiores percentuais foram observados no Sudeste (22,7%) e no Centro-Oeste (21,7%).

O Sudeste concentrou 15,1 milhões dos 32,9 milhões de eleitores que não compareceram às urnas no Brasil, desconsiderando os eleitores no exterior.

Outro dado destacado pelo pesquisador é que a abstenção no Nordeste caiu de 19,5%, em 2022, para 18,4% neste ano. Na comparação entre as duas eleições, o número de pessoas que compareceram às urnas na região aumentou em 1,4 milhão.

Nicolau ressalta, no entanto, que os números precisam ser analisados com cautela. Em 2026, 716 municípios tinham mais eleitores cadastrados do que habitantes, situação que pode distorcer as taxas de abstenção.

Isso acontece, por exemplo, quando uma pessoa muda de cidade sem transferir o título ou quando eleitores que morreram ainda permanecem no cadastro eleitoral.

Quem são os brasileiros que deixam de votar?

Para entender o perfil dos eleitores ausentes, Nicolau analisou dados das três eleições anteriores, reunidos em seu livro "O País Dividido". Os dados detalhados sobre o perfil social dos eleitores que não votaram em 2026 ainda não foram divulgados e devem ser disponibilizados após o segundo turno.

O estudo identificou dois grupos importantes entre os eleitores que não comparecem às urnas:

Jovens de 18 a 29 anos , para quem o voto é obrigatório.

Pessoas com 70 anos ou mais , especialmente mulheres de baixa escolaridade, que não são obrigadas a votar.

Entre os jovens, o número de ausentes surpreendeu o pesquisador. No primeiro turno de 2022, 7,7 milhões de eleitores de 18 a 29 anos deixaram de votar — 4,3 milhões de homens e 3,5 milhões de mulheres.

👉🏻Outro dado que chamou a atenção de Nicolau foi a alta abstenção de jovens que tiram o título de eleitor aos 16 ou 17 anos, quando o voto ainda é facultativo, e não comparecem às urnas.

Segundo ele, os jovens estão entre os grupos que podem ser mais facilmente mobilizados para votar no segundo turno, diferentemente de parte dos eleitores idosos, que enfrentam dificuldades de deslocamento ou problemas de saúde.

📍Na outra ponta, cerca de três em cada dez eleitores ausentes nas eleições anteriores não eram obrigados a votar. São pessoas com 70 anos ou mais e analfabetos de qualquer idade.

Entre os idosos, destacam-se as mulheres de baixa escolaridade. Em 2022, aproximadamente 4,5 milhões de mulheres com 70 anos ou mais, analfabetas ou com escolaridade até o ensino fundamental, não compareceram às urnas.

O pesquisador ressalta que parte dessas ausências está associada a dificuldades de locomoção, problemas de saúde e distância até os locais de votação. Há ainda pessoas que deixaram de votar há muitos anos e continuam no cadastro eleitoral.

Por isso, segundo Nicolau, não é possível tratar todos os ausentes como eleitores que decidiram rejeitar a política ou os candidatos.

Outro ponto levantado pelo pesquisador é que, embora o voto seja obrigatório no Brasil para pessoas entre 18 e 70 anos, as consequências práticas de não comparecer às urnas são relativamente pequenas.

Nicolau cita a facilidade para justificar a ausência pelo celular e o baixo valor da multa eleitoral, de R$ 3,70, inferior ao preço de uma passagem de ônibus em muitas cidades.

Na avaliação dele, isso faz com que a obrigatoriedade do voto tenha perdido parte de seu efeito prático.

“É um voto obrigatório no papel, mas está se tornando um voto facultativo na prática”, afirmou.

O pesquisador ressalta que não defende o aumento da multa. Para ele, o mais importante é compreender as diferentes razões pelas quais os eleitores deixam de votar.

A falta de pesquisas específicas sobre esse público, segundo Nicolau, ainda impede uma compreensão mais precisa do fenômeno.

Abstenção no primeiro turno chegou a 21%, maior índice já registrado — Foto: Eliandra Bussinger

articles.title: Judge orders cancellation of Trump’s government-funded ads
articles.summary: A federal judge on Sunday told the Trump administration its new ads featuring the president are likely unlawful and must stop — including any set to be aired later in the day. The administration had indicated the ad campaign is set to end on Sunday, so there was no need for the judge to intervene. In…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Sunday told the Trump administration its new ads featuring the president are likely unlawful and must stop — including any set to be aired later in the day.

The administration had indicated the ad campaign is set to end on Sunday, so there was no need for the judge to intervene.

In a four-page order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found the dispute wasn’t moot and that the unions and others suing were likely to succeed in their challenge.

Rochon’s order requires the government to not disburse any more funds and cancel any remaining ad reservations, “including those placements for the evening of October 11.” She said her ruling took effect 6:45 p.m. EDT, and it lasts for two weeks.

Rochon is an appointee of former President Biden who serves in New York City.

The Trump administration launched the ad campaign promoting the president in the final weeks leading up to the midterm elections. One of the ads shows images and clips of Trump overlaid by quotes from recent speeches demeaning communism while also crediting himself for the largest tax cuts in history.

The campaign is paid for through funding earmarked for U.S. Customs and Border Protection. In court filings, the administration indicated the ads have cost nearly $20 million.

The ads face multiple lawsuits, but Rochon’s ruling is the first known time that a judge has blocked them.

She oversees a suit brought by Common Cause, unions and an Alabama state house candidate. The Democratic National Committee and the party’s Wisconsin arm have also sued separately.

The challengers say the administration unlawfully repurposed funds Congress appropriated for another purpose and that the ads amount to improper use of taxpayer funds for “political propaganda.”

“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs reacted to Sunday’s ruling in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”

The Trump administration told Rochon that the challengers had no right to sue, they improperly filed the suit in New York and that they wouldn’t face irreparable harm since the campaign is set to end Sunday. The government’s filing did not, however, focus on defending the actual legality of the ads.

The Hill has reached out to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson for comment.

“The Department has directed the Vendor not to make any additional media buys past October 11 and expects that the Vendor will submit its final invoice,” Holly Mehringer, who currently performs the duties of DHS’s CFO, wrote to the judge on Saturday .

images.caption: President Donald Trump speaks with reporters as he arrives on Air Force One, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

articles.title: Federal judge orders pro-Trump TV ads funded by taxpayers off air immediately
articles.summary: In an earlier filing, the administration said it had planned to stop ad purchases Sunday.
articles.body: A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Sunday to stop airing ads funded by the U.S. government that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, effective immediately. The lawsuit was brought by the watchdog group Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House; and a labor union in New York and its political action committee. The suit was one of several similar complaints — including one by the Democratic National Committee — that were filed to get the ads off the air. “Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest,” U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York wrote. The administration had said in a court filing Saturday that the Department of Homeland Security, via a vendor, had placed ad buys through Sunday and had told the vendor to not purchase ads beyond that day. Rochon said the plaintiffs’ argument was not moot, however, and ordered the Trump administration to “cancel or cause to be cancelled” any ads from airing or being disseminated, including those set to air Sunday night. Rochon also wrote that the administration was barred from using funds appropriated to DHS to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged advertisements.” The White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget, which are all named as defendants in the suit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling. MAGA Inc., which Trump had said last week would help him fund the ads moving forward, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.” Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said that despite the ruling, “our fight continues.” “We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” Solomón said. The ads — one of which was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — came under scrutiny by critics who argued that using taxpayer money could be illegal and called the spots propaganda.

images.caption: President Donald Trump speaks during an election rally at the Oncenter on October 09, 2026 in Syracuse, New York.

articles.title: Trump says new press secretary to hold first press conference next week
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday that his new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press conference next week. “I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday that his new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press conference next week.

“I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the Press Briefing Room in the White House. Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!” Trump said in a Sunday evening Truth Social post.

Trump recently named Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Trump Media communications adviser, as the next White House press secretary.

“She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7. She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning,” the president said in a Truth Social post on Friday.

The New York Times was the first to report of Zacharia’s selection for the role.

Zacharia is set to step into a job vacated by Trump ally Karoline Leavitt, who stepped away from the administration earlier this year following the birth of her second child. She also took a job as a Fox News commentator.

Zacharia has previously held roles as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and a top communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social.

The former DHS spokesperson is the second press secretary in Trump’s second term and the sixth consecutive woman to hold the role.

“The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day,” Zacharia said in a prior post on the social platform X.

images.caption: Katie Zacharia on December 14, 2025 in Franklin, Tenn (left). The White House press briefing room (right). (Terry Wyatt/Getty Images for 2521 Entertainment and Angel Studios/AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)

articles.title: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran war, AI and Trump in fiery debate
articles.summary: Annie Andrews and Darline Graham are running to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, and the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina.
articles.body: Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed Sunday night in their first and perhaps only debate of the general election, tangling over President Donald Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill,” the high costs of gas and goods, the Iran war and AI data centers. South Carolina is a ruby-red state where Trump remains popular among Republican voters. But the race has tightened in the closing stretch of the campaign, and Democrats believe they have a shot at knocking off Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat after his sudden death in July. The top Senate Republican super PAC has pledged to spend $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign. At the start of the debate, hosted in Columbia by South Carolina ETV, Darline Graham noted that Sunday night marked exactly three months since her brother unexpectedly died at age 71. Andrews, a pediatrician, sought to portray Graham, who previously led a state agency, as an inexperienced empty suit who refuses to stand up to Trump or his unpopular policies. She mocked Graham as “the White House’s ambassador to South Carolina.” Graham attacked Andrews as the “most radical liberal” to run in South Carolina and as sympathetic to the Democratic Socialist Party. “Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party; she’s only going to join them,” Graham said — a characterization Andrews rejected. Graham has “been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani — that’s what’s in her script. But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that,” Andrews said. “The truth is I support the Second Amendment, I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law. ... The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party, and I will always put South Carolina first.” Graham and Andrews are running for a full six-year Senate term; the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina. The debate also featured Libertarian Kasie Whitener. Graham and Andrews tussled over issue after issue. As the country faces Social Security insolvency, Andrews said she would raise caps to make wealthier people pay more but would not hike the retirement age. She added that Republicans like Graham want to privatize Social Security so “Washington insiders” can profit. “Unfortunately, my opponent is in the race to do what Washington insiders tell her,” she said. Graham shot back that she understands what people in her state are facing. When her parents died at a young age, Social Security benefits helped her and her brother survive. Graham said Andrews’ criticism of Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” is misplaced because it lowered taxes on tips and Social Security. “You called it the one big, ugly bill, so here you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham said. On affordability, Graham said she has “lived paycheck to paycheck” before and acknowledged that “gas prices are high right now. ... I feel the pain, too.” She said that she supports suspending the gas tax and that easing regulations on drilling would permanently bring prices down. Andrews pinned blame for high gas prices on Graham, who she said voted several times against a war powers resolution to restrict Trump’s war with Iran. “The war is the exact reason we now have record-high gas and diesel prices. Farmers are getting crushed, and everything costs more,” Andrews said. “My opponent is the only one who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it.” Andrews also dinged Graham for admitting during a previous debate that “national security is not my thing.” “South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the U.S. Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.” Graham retorted that she wants the war to end, like everyone does, but said she believes in “peace through strength.” Then, she went after Andrews over the national security quip. “But talking about not my thing, let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” Graham said without getting specific. “But you have, you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove it. Shame on you!” The proliferation of data centers, which power artificial intelligence companies, has become a major flash point in the midterm elections. Andrews went right after Graham on the issue, nicknaming her “Data Center Darline.” Andrews said her data-center plan calls for a “two-year moratorium, protections to ensure your rates don’t go up and a return to real local control.” Graham fired back that stopping construction of all data centers would allow China to win the race for AI dominance. She said she voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to shift higher energy costs from building data centers from consumers onto AI companies. “Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country, because in two years China is going to be so far ahead [that] we are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said, adding that local communities should decide whether data centers get built in their backyards. “I want communities to decide. She wants the federal government to decide.”

images.caption: Democrat Annie Andrews and Sen. Darline Graham.

articles.title: Lone debate for South Carolina Senate gets testy: 5 takeaways
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R) and pediatrician Annie Andrews (D) faced off in their one and only debate on Sunday in the South Carolina Senate race, which quickly became testy as Graham sought to tie the physician to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while Andrews suggested the GOP senator wouldn’t be able to stand up…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R) and pediatrician Annie Andrews (D) faced off in their one and only debate on Sunday in the South Carolina Senate race, which quickly became testy as Graham sought to tie the physician to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while Andrews suggested the GOP senator wouldn’t be able to stand up to the White House.

Graham, Andrews and libertarian Kasie Whitener, a radio host and professor, participated in a debate hosted by South Carolina ETV and Public Radio (SCETV) in Columbia, S.C.

Graham suggested Andrews was in favor of progressive policies like Medicare for All and called her a “radical liberal.”

Meanwhile, Andrews pointed to Graham’s past primary debate gaffe on Taiwan as reason why the GOP senator was not up to the task of a full six-year term and dinged her for dropping “Nordone” from her last name.

Graham is seen as the favorite to win in November, with Decision Desk HQ forecasting a 70 percent probability that the GOP senator wins next month.

Here are 5 takeaways from the South Carolina Senate’s lone debate:

Graham, Andrews take swipes at each other

Graham and Andrews set the tone for the debate early, taking swipes at each other on policy issues and even their own personal names.

“I’ve been in the Senate for three months now. I’ve already co-sponsored several bills that protect farmers, that protect the American taxpayer,” the GOP senator said just minutes into the debate. “My Democratic opponent is pretending to be someone she is not. She’s the most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina.”

Graham also suggested that Andrews, a pediatrician, supported “government-run health care for all.”

“We are already $40 trillion in national debt. That will cost trillions of dollars,” Graham continued. “Our national debt will be through the roof. She will bankrupt our country with government-run healthcare for all.”

The Senate Democratic candidate called Medicare for All in August “a policy from a few decades ago,” saying she was in favor of creating a public option for the Affordable Care Act (ACA).

Meanwhile, Andrews dinged Graham for dropping “Nordone” from her name after joining the Senate, insinuating that she was trying to ride on the tailcoats of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R) name.

“I told you my opponent was going to call me a socialist, and there she’s done it again. She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani. That’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said. “But the truth is, my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.”

Graham slammed Andrews over the statement, saying the name “Graham” appears in all of her signed documents and said she kept the name to feel close to her parents who died when she was young.

The Democratic pediatrician also suggested Graham wouldn’t be able to stand up to the president or White House while in the upper chamber.

“The job is to represent South Carolina. She considers the job to be to read their scripts and do their bidding, and we can do better,” Andrews said.

Andrews referenced a gaffe the GOP senator made during her primary runoff debate against Rep. Ralph Norman (R) in which she said that national security “is not my thing,” suggesting that the GOP senator lacked the experience needed to do the job.

“My opponent is the only one on this stage who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it,” Andrews said at one point in response to a question about the war with Iran. “And several days after one of those votes, she had the audacity to walk out onto this stage and admit that national security isn’t really her thing. South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No.”

During a debate between Graham and Norman in August, the GOP senator was asked a national security question pertaining to Taiwan and the South China Sea.

“I’m just going to be honest here. … I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham said, adding later, “but I do support the military.”

Graham defended herself afterward , saying that “I’m not a politician” and that voters care more about domestic issues than those abroad. The GOP senator defended herself again on the debate stage, saying that constituents respected that she was honest about what she did and did not know.

“Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina,” Graham shot back. “At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight. But … you are deceiving the people of South Carolina.”

Andrews presses Graham to commit to more debates

The pediatrician pressed Graham twice to commit to another debate between the pair, arguing that voters should hear from the candidates again before the election, which is three weeks away.

“There’s a lot to talk about in this U.S. Senate race, and unfortunately, my opponent has only agreed to this one 60-minute debate. I’ve agreed to three additional debates. We have a lot to talk about. That is very clear,” Andrews said. “So I want to ask Senator Graham this evening if she’ll commit to standing on another debate stage with me at least two more times before Nov. 3?”

Graham brushed off the request after she was pressed a second time.

“I’ve had a job representing the people of South Carolina in Washington, D.C., so I think it’s more important for me to hear from voters than to stand with you on this debate stage,” Graham said.

Graham sidesteps question on Trump deal with Russia on diesel

The GOP senator sidestepped a question about whether she supported a recent deal the president made with Russia on diesel. Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply the U.S. and the global marketplace with 300,000 tons of diesel “immediately.”

The move marked a reverse on legislation the president had signed into law in September , which was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R), that placed as much as 100-percent tariffs on Russia’s top energy buyers.

The president fielded blowback from his deal with Russia from both parties.

“I think that everybody wants the war in Ukraine to end. We will all be safer when the war in Ukraine ends,” Graham said during the debate, saying she was “proud” to help pass the legislation that enacted stricter sanctions.

“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses to end the war through economic sanctions. So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it or whether he wants to use something else,” she said. “But I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”

The GOP senator sought to tie Andrews to the far-left multiple times during the debate as Republicans have largely looked to make the midterms a referendum on democratic socialists and the progressive faction of the party.

“Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party. She’s only going to join them,” Graham said at one point, criticizing the response from some progressive Democrats to the Oct. 7, 2023 attack against Israel.

Andrews accused Graham of using the name-calling as a distraction.

“My opponent is going to stand up here tonight and call me a socialist because that’s what her script says,” Andrews said, “and also because she doesn’t want to talk to you about your high gas prices, grocery prices or your closing rural hospital.”

articles.title: FIR against Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani over obstruction, rioting at Gujarat police station during poll campaign
articles.summary: GANDHINAGAR: An FIR has been registered against Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani at Pethapur police station in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar over allegations of
articles.body: GANDHINAGAR: An FIR has been registered against Congress MLA Jignesh Mevani at Pethapur police station in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar over allegations of obstructing police personnel while they were recording a statement from a Congress candidate during the election campaign on October 9.According to the FIR, police were recording the candidate’s statement in connection with a complaint received against him when Mevani arrived at the police station with his supporters and allegedly obstructed personnel from discharging their duties.Mevani booked under multiple BNS sectionsThe FIR invokes several provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including Section 189(2), which deals with punishment for unlawful assembly; Section 190, concerning joint liability for acts committed by members of an unlawful assembly; and Section 191(2), which relates to rioting.Other sections invoked include Section 221 for obstructing a public servant in the discharge of duties; Section 351(2) for criminal intimidation; and Section 352 for intentional insult with intent to provoke a breach of peace.The FIR also includes Section 353(1)(b), concerning the spread of rumours or false statements intended to cause public fear or panic; Section 353(1)(c), concerning false information intended to incite one community or class to commit an offence against another; and Section 353(2), which deals with promoting enmity, hatred or ill-will between different groups on specified grounds.What does the FIR allege?According to the FIR, the incident took place on October 9 at Pethapur police station in Gandhinagar during an election campaign.Police were recording a statement from a Congress candidate regarding a complaint received against him when Mevani allegedly arrived with his supporters and obstructed the officers in the discharge of their duties.Further details about the investigation and the allegations against Mevani were not available in the information provided.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ahmedabad | Silver Rate in Ahmedabad | Bank Holidays in Ahmedabad | Public Holidays in Ahmedabad | Ahmedabad AQI | Weather in Ahmedabad | Petrol Price in Ahmedabad | Diesel Price in Ahmedabad | CNG Price in Ahmedabad | LPG Price in AhmedabadStay updated with the latest Ahmedabad news. articles.title: ‘I just had the flu’: James Talarico shoots down conservative speculation about his absence from the trail
articles.summary: In an interview with NBC Dallas-Fort Worth, the Democrat again challenged his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, to a debate in the Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico addressed his recent absence from the campaign trail Sunday, saying it was nothing but a “nasty case of the flu.” “I was in bed, drinking lots of liquids. Unfortunately, the campaign made me work from home, so I didn’t even get full days off. But I didn’t want to be out on the trail, and I didn’t want to get anyone else sick. It’s important, I think, for leaders to be responsible in these moments. And I’m glad to be back. I’m feeling much better,” he told NBC Dallas-Fort Worth in an interview. Talarico returned to the campaign trail Friday; his last in-person event in the state had been Sept. 26, and on Sept. 30, he spoke at a forum virtually, saying he wasn’t feeling well. In his absence, some conservatives speculated that he was taking a break for mental health reasons. One right-wing influencer falsely claimed Talarico was receiving treatment at the Lindner Center of Hope, a facility in Ohio. Asked about those theories, Talarico said, “The internet’s doing its thing.” “That’s not true,” Talarico said. “I just had the flu, and I feel much better. But it’s a good reminder that you can’t believe everything you read on the internet.” The Lindner Center also shot down the speculation Sunday, posting on social media: “Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope.” Republicans latched on to Talarico’s being off the trail in the final weeks of the campaign, and even some Democrats admitted to NBC News that his absence was less than ideal in the tight Senate race. State Attorney General Ken Paxton, Talarico’s Republican opponent, called for him to show “proof of life” with a picture of him and a newspaper showing the date. President Donald Trump, stumping for Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday, highlighted Talarico’s absence and urged him to debate Paxton. Asked about Trump’s comment Sunday, Talarico said he agreed. “I agree with President Trump. I think Ken Paxton should debate. The president’s saying he should debate. Fox News has said he should debate. The people of Texas have said he should debate, and I think it’s mysterious that Ken Paxton hasn’t responded to a request for a debate in 85 days,” Talarico said. “Ken Paxton has asked for proof of life for me. I’m asking for proof of spine from him,” he added. So far, no debates are scheduled. Talarico has accepted debate invitations from multiple media outlets, but Paxton hasn’t done the same.
